newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Businessman tells inquiry he paid Irish ex-premier.
newsitem.headline: Businessman tells inquiry he paid Irish ex-premier.

text.p: An Irish businessman told a tribunal investigating cash payments to politicians on Monday that he gave former prime minister Charles Haughey money to "help him out of financial difficulties".
Ben Dunne was giving evidence on the first day of an investigation into payments which have claimed one political scalp and brought the whiff of scandal to an election year.

Dunne, a member of the family that controls the Dunne's department store chain that has stores in every Irish high street, acknowledged paying 200,000 pounds ($320,000) to Haughey through a Cayman Islands bank account.
Haughey was Irish prime minister four times between 1979 and 1992.

Dunne, who was dropped by the rest of the Dunne family in 1993 in a family row, said he was told by an associate of Haughey that the former premier needed 700,000 pounds to ease him out of financial straits.

Earlier the counsel for the tribunal, Dennis McCullough, told the judge that Haughey, one of the stars of the Irish political firmament, received a total of 1.3 million pounds ($2 million) from Dunne between 1987 and 1991.
It was the first time Haughey had been officially named in the affair. To date, he has said nothing except a one-line denial that he ever received money in a Cork-based newspaper.
Michael Lowry, a rising star in the ruling Fine Gael party of Prime Minister John Bruton, quit last year when a newspaper broke the story that Dunne had paid for the renovation of his Tipperary home.
McCullough said Dunne would testify that he gave Lowry up to 200,000 pounds because of business relationship between Dunne's stores and a refrigeration company owned by Lowry.
In addition, Dunne paid much of the 350,000-pound bill for the renovation of Lowry's house which included the cost of "furniture, paintings and a custom-built double bed".
But media interest in the tribunal has centred on allegations that Dunne paid money to Haughey of the Fianna Fail party, the most powerful political force in Ireland.
"The evidence which Mr Dunne will give is that between December 1987 and November 1991 he arranged for 1.3 million pounds to be paid to the benefit of Charles J. Haughey," he said.
McCullough said there was no suggestion that money paid to either Haughey or Lowry or any other figures to be named in the investigation was to buy political favours.

But the news that a millionaire Irish businessman had given cash to an assortment of politicians and political parties has raised calls for a new code governing funding of political parties and more transparency.

Haughey, who has been in virtual retirement since he stepped down as prime minister in 1992, has said nothing publicly about the allegations, which coincide with the run-up to national elections due by November.
But Bertie Ahern, current Fianna Fail leader, moved at the weekend to distance himself from a one-time mentor who dominated Irish politics for more than a decade.

Ahern told a weekend party conference that anyone named by the tribunal should be presumed innocent until proven guilty but said he would not tolerate unethical conduct. Ahern wants the tribunal to carry out its work before Bruton calls an election so that all politicians and parties named by it will have to testify before the poll.
